passages.title: The Stripes That Changed Shopping
passages.body:
**A**  In the late 1960s, queues at American supermarkets were getting longer. Cashiers typed every price by hand, which was slow and easy to get wrong. A committee of food retailers asked several companies to design a better system, and the winning proposal came from an engineer at IBM named George Laurer. His design used a pattern of black and white bars to represent a number. The Universal Product Code, as it became known, was adopted in 1973, and the first item was scanned in a supermarket in Troy, Ohio, in June 1974: a packet of chewing gum.

**B**  The stripes do not contain the price. They encode a short number that identifies the product, and the checkout computer looks up the price in the store's database. This is why the same bar code can be used in different shops with different prices. A laser reads the pattern as the item passes over a glass window, and a check digit at the end of the number lets the system detect most reading errors.

**C**  The effects reached far beyond the checkout. Because every sale was now recorded automatically, shops could see exactly what was selling and when, and manufacturers could track their products through warehouses and delivery trucks. Loyalty cards later linked that data to individual customers, which raised concerns about how much shops could learn about people's habits.

**D**  Newer systems have appeared. QR codes can hold far more data than a row of stripes, and RFID tags use radio waves to identify items without a line of sight. Yet the ordinary barcode survives because it is extremely cheap: printing one costs almost nothing, and a basic reader is inexpensive. For most packaged goods, it remains the simplest tool that works.

questions.prompt: The barcode was invented to make supermarket checkouts faster.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A describes long queues and hand-typed prices as the problem.

questions.prompt: The first barcode was scanned in 1973.
questions.explanation: The code was adopted in 1973, but the first scan was in June 1974.

questions.prompt: The stripes contain the price of the product.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says the stripes encode a product number; the price is looked up in a database.

questions.prompt: QR codes have completely replaced barcodes.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says the ordinary barcode survives because it is so cheap.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a check digit?
questions.explanation: Paragraph B: a check digit lets the system detect most reading errors.

questions.prompt: What was the first product scanned?
questions.explanation: Paragraph A: a packet of chewing gum.

questions.prompt: What concern does the passage mention?
options: Shops can learn a lot about customers' habits.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C mentions loyalty cards and concerns about what shops could learn.

questions.instructions: Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B: a laser reads the pattern.

questions.prompt: RFID tags use radio waves rather than a line of ______.
questions.instructions: Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D: without a line of sight.

questions.explanation: Paragraph A says the code was adopted in 1973.
